prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

(CNN) -- Canadian ski resort gondola cars that were left dangling and swaying with terrified skiers inside failed because ice buildup snapped a supporting tower, the resort said Thursday. One gondola car is suspended above an icy creek at a ski resort near Whistler, British Columbia. In a rare occurrence called ice-jacking, water seeped into the lower section of the lift tower and turned to ice Tuesday at Whistler Blackcomb resort, 177 kilometers (110 miles) north of Vancouver, a resort official said in a press release Thursday. The lift hangs from a tower that is spliced into two parts. Extremely cold temperatures caused the ice buildup that exerted 800 tons of pressure between the two parts that hold the tower together, causing them to rupture, according to Whistler Blackcomb. The section of the lift affected by the accident had 15 cars going up the mountain and 15 coming down at the time, but they weren't carrying a lot of passengers, according to Doug Forseth, senior vice president of the resort. He said 53 passengers had been rescued from the stranded cars. No skiers at the Whistler, British Columbia, resort were seriously injured. "The towers are not normally designed to allow for any water penetration and so this failure is a very unusual situation," said Warren Sparks, senior vice president of Doppelmayr Canada, the engineering firm that investigated the accident. They are trying to figure out what caused the water to pool. He said independent structural engineers are examining the tower from Vancouver-based CVMM Consulting Engineers. "The evidence so far indicates a sudden rupture rather than a fatigue failure over an extended period," Sparks said. At least two gondola cars broke away and hit the ground, both from relatively low heights near the tower that split, and caused the system's heavy cable line to slacken, according to Tyler Noble, a reporter for CNNRadio affiliate CKNW in Vancouver. "One hit a bus stop and the other hit a house," Noble said Wednesday. "Another one was suspended over a creek, but everyone is out of that car." The broken Excaliber Gondola was not operating Thursday. Whistler engineers checked eight similar towers across the two mountains of the resort. All passed those inspections, and are open Thursday, the release said. The British Columbia Authority says it does not expect to rescind operating permits on any lifts at the resort, other than the Excaliber Gondola. Jeff Colburn, general manager of Silver Mountain Resort in Kellogg, Idaho, said a lift tower at his resort was similarly damaged by ice in December 2006. The damage was discovered in the morning before the slopes opened, so no one was endangered, he said. The damaged tower was replaced in about three weeks, Colburn said, and the resort's business was not significantly disrupted. "We check our towers in the summer now, and we also check before we open up for ski season as well just to make sure they don't have any water in them, and we've worked with the manufacturers," he said. Holes have been drilled in the bases of towers so that water can drain out, Colburn said. CNN's Ashley Fantz and Jim Kavanagh contributed to this report.

In a rare phenomenon known as ice-jacking, water seeped into the lower section of a lift tower and froze Tuesday at Whistler Blackcomb resort, 177 kilometers (110 miles) north of Vancouver, a resort official said in a news release Thursday.

The lift is supported by a tower spliced into two sections. According to Whistler Blackcomb, extremely cold temperatures caused ice to accumulate and exert 800 tons of pressure between the two sections holding the tower together, causing them to rupture.

At the time of the accident, the affected section of the lift had 15 cars traveling up the mountain and 15 coming down, though they were carrying relatively few passengers, said Doug Forseth, the resort’s senior vice president. He said 53 passengers were rescued from the stranded cars. No skiers at the Whistler, British Columbia, resort were seriously injured.

“The towers are not normally designed to allow for any water penetration, and so this failure is a very unusual situation,” said Warren Sparks, senior vice president of Doppelmayr Canada, the engineering firm that investigated the accident.

Investigators are working to determine what caused the water to pool. Sparks said independent structural engineers from Vancouver-based CVMM Consulting Engineers are examining the tower.

“The evidence so far indicates a sudden rupture rather than a fatigue failure over an extended period,” Sparks said.

At least two gondola cars broke away and struck the ground. Both fell from relatively low heights near the tower that split, causing the system’s heavy cable line to slacken, according to Tyler Noble, a reporter for CNNRadio affiliate CKNW in Vancouver.

“One hit a bus stop and the other hit a house,” Noble said Wednesday. “Another one was suspended over a creek, but everyone is out of that car.”

The damaged Excaliber Gondola was not operating Thursday. Whistler engineers inspected eight similar towers across the resort’s two mountains. All passed inspection and were open Thursday, according to the release.

The British Columbia Authority said it did not expect to rescind operating permits for any lifts at the resort other than the Excaliber Gondola.

Jeff Colburn, general manager of Silver Mountain Resort in Kellogg, Idaho, said a lift tower at his resort sustained similar ice damage in December 2006. Because the damage was discovered in the morning before the slopes opened, no one was endangered, he said.

The damaged tower was replaced in about three weeks, Colburn said, and the resort’s business was not significantly disrupted.

“We check our towers in the summer now, and we also check before we open up for ski season as well, just to make sure they don’t have any water in them, and we’ve worked with the manufacturers,” he said.

outputs.L2:
(CNN) — A rare accumulation of ice caused a support tower to break at a Canadian ski resort, leaving frightened passengers trapped in gondola cabins that swung above the ground, resort officials said Thursday. One cabin remained hanging over a frozen creek near Whistler, British Columbia.

According to a Thursday statement from a resort representative, water entered the bottom portion of a lift tower at Whistler Blackcomb on Tuesday and froze in a phenomenon known as “ice-jacking.” The resort is located 177 kilometers (110 miles) north of Vancouver.

The tower consists of two joined sections. Whistler Blackcomb said exceptionally cold weather froze the trapped water, generating about 800 tons of force between the components connecting the two sections and ultimately breaking them apart.

Doug Forseth, the resort’s senior vice president, said the affected part of the lift had 15 cabins traveling uphill and another 15 descending when the failure occurred. The cabins were carrying relatively few people, and rescuers evacuated 53 passengers. No one at the Whistler resort suffered serious injuries.

Warren Sparks, senior vice president of Doppelmayr Canada, the engineering company investigating the incident, said lift towers ordinarily are built to prevent water from getting inside, making this type of failure highly unusual. Investigators are working to determine why water collected there.

Independent structural specialists from Vancouver-based CVMM Consulting Engineers are also inspecting the tower. Sparks said the available evidence points to an abrupt break, rather than damage caused by long-term fatigue.

At least two gondola cabins detached and fell from comparatively low elevations close to the broken tower, according to Tyler Noble, a reporter with Vancouver CNNRadio affiliate CKNW. The tower failure also caused the system’s heavy cable to lose tension.

Noble said Wednesday that one cabin struck a bus stop and another landed on a house. A third was left hanging above a creek, but all of its occupants were safely removed.

The damaged Excaliber Gondola remained closed Thursday. Engineers at Whistler examined eight comparable towers on the resort’s two mountains. The resort’s statement said all eight passed inspection and were operating Thursday.

The British Columbia Authority said it did not anticipate revoking operating permits for any resort lifts apart from the Excaliber Gondola.

A similar ice-related incident damaged a lift tower at Silver Mountain Resort in Kellogg, Idaho, in December 2006, according to general manager Jeff Colburn. Because employees found the problem in the morning before the ski runs opened, nobody was placed in danger.

Colburn said the tower was replaced in roughly three weeks, with little effect on the resort’s business. Since then, the resort has worked with manufacturers and inspects its towers during the summer and again before the ski season to ensure that no water has collected inside. Drainage holes have also been drilled into the tower bases to allow water to escape, he said.

CNN’s Ashley Fantz and Jim Kavanagh contributed to this report.

**Gondola tower collapse at Whistler Blackcomb blamed on ‘ice jacking’**

**WHISTLER, British Columbia —** A rare buildup of ice inside a lift tower caused the dramatic collapse of part of the Excalibur Gondola at Whistler Blackcomb ski resort, investigators said.

The accident occurred on December 16, 2008, when a section of a gondola support tower failed near the resort’s village area. Several passenger cabins dropped or swung violently after the cable sagged, leaving about a dozen people with injuries, most of them minor. Dozens of others were stranded and rescued from the line.

Investigators determined that water had entered the hollow steel tower and frozen. As the water expanded, it forced apart a connection in a process known as **ice jacking**, weakening the structure until it separated.

Witnesses described gondola cabins plunging toward the ground and striking trees, buildings or a nearby bus shelter. Emergency crews used ladders and other equipment to remove passengers as the resort shut down the lift and secured the area.

The incident prompted inspections of similar towers and changes intended to prevent water from accumulating inside lift structures. Whistler Blackcomb later repaired the damaged equipment and returned the gondola to service after receiving regulatory approval.

The collapse drew international attention because it happened during the busy winter season, little more than a year before Whistler hosted alpine events for the 2010 Vancouver Winter Olympics. No fatalities were reported.

# Ice Buildup Generated 800 Tons of Pressure, Rupturing Lift Tower at Whistler Blackcomb

**WHISTLER, British Columbia — Dec. 17, 2008** — Ice expanding inside a supporting tower generated an estimated 800 tons of pressure before rupturing the structure and causing a gondola failure at Whistler Blackcomb, according to preliminary findings released after Tuesday’s accident.

The failure occurred on the Excalibur Gondola, which carries passengers from Whistler Village toward Blackcomb Mountain. A section of one steel support tower split apart, allowing the gondola cable to sag and leaving several cabins suspended unusually close to the ground and nearby buildings.

Emergency crews evacuated passengers from the stranded cabins. Several people were taken to hospital with injuries, but authorities reported no fatalities.

Investigators believe water entered the hollow steel tower and subsequently froze. As the water expanded, it created an “ice-jacking” effect, exerting enormous internal force on the tower’s welded or bolted connection. Officials estimated that the resulting pressure reached the equivalent of roughly 800 tons—enough to rupture the structural joint.

The tower did not topple in the manner of a conventional structural collapse. Instead, the expanding ice forced apart a connection in the steel column, compromising the tower and causing its upper section to buckle.

Whistler Blackcomb closed the Excalibur Gondola immediately after the incident and began inspecting similar towers and lift infrastructure across the resort. Engineers and safety regulators were expected to examine how moisture entered the tower, whether drainage or sealing systems failed, and whether the defect could have been detected during routine inspections.

Resort officials said passenger safety remained their highest priority and that the gondola would not reopen until engineers completed a full assessment and authorized its return to service.

The accident came during the early part of the ski season, when freezing temperatures and changing weather conditions can place significant stress on mountain infrastructure. Ice accumulation is common at high-elevation resorts, but internal freezing inside a sealed structural component is considered an unusual and potentially difficult-to-detect hazard.

The Excalibur Gondola is a major access route serving Blackcomb Mountain. Its closure was expected to disrupt normal operations, although other lifts and routes remained available.

Authorities cautioned that the 800-ton figure was an engineering estimate of the force created inside the tower, not the weight of ice present. The final cause, including any contributing maintenance, design or manufacturing issues, remained subject to a formal investigation.

# Tower failure strands 53 passengers on Whistler’s Excalibur Gondola

**WHISTLER, British Columbia —** A structural failure on Whistler Blackcomb’s Excalibur Gondola left 53 passengers suspended in cabins and prompted a large-scale rescue, as safety officials began inspecting other ski lifts for signs of the freezing-related problem blamed for the accident.

The failure occurred Dec. 16, 2008, on the lower section of the gondola, which carries passengers from Whistler Village toward Blackcomb Mountain. A steel support tower buckled, causing the haul rope to sag and several cabins to drop or swing violently.

Some cabins remained high above the ground, including one near Fitzsimmons Creek, while others came down closer to buildings and resort infrastructure. Emergency crews used ladders, ropes and aerial-rescue equipment to reach the passengers. All 53 people were eventually removed from the line.

A dozen people were taken to hospitals or treated for injuries, according to authorities. None of the injuries was reported to be life-threatening.

Investigators focused on a phenomenon known as “ice jacking.” Water can enter a hollow steel lift tower through an opening or inadequately sealed connection. When temperatures fall, the trapped water freezes and expands, creating enough internal pressure to split or deform the steel.

The failed Excalibur tower showed evidence consistent with that process. Officials said the problem could develop out of sight because the ice forms inside the structure, making ordinary exterior inspections less likely to detect it.

The accident led Whistler Blackcomb and provincial safety authorities to examine other lift towers, particularly those with similar hollow-steel construction. Inspections included checks for cracks, openings that could allow water inside and signs of internal ice accumulation. Other lifts were cleared individually before being returned to service, while the affected section of the Excalibur Gondola remained closed for repairs and further investigation.

The review extended beyond the immediate accident site because ice jacking was already a known, though uncommon, hazard in the ski industry.

A similar tower failure occurred in 2006 at Silver Mountain Resort near Kellogg, Idaho. Investigators there also concluded that water had entered a hollow lift tower and frozen, building pressure until the steel structure failed. That incident became an important comparison for Canadian investigators examining the Excalibur accident and reinforced concerns that the danger could exist in towers that appeared sound from the outside.

Following the Whistler failure, operators were urged to ensure that hollow towers were properly sealed and drained and to use more intensive inspection methods where necessary. The accident also highlighted the importance of evacuation planning: although the damaged line left dozens of people stranded in cold conditions and difficult terrain, rescuers were able to remove every passenger without a fatality.

The Excalibur Gondola, whose name is sometimes misspelled “Excaliber,” is a major connection between Whistler Village and Blackcomb Mountain. The tower failure was one of the resort’s most serious lift accidents and led to increased scrutiny of lift-tower design, maintenance and inspection practices across the region.
